title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics
book_title: The Plumbing of 3X Leverage: Creation Units, Swap Supply Chains, and Fee Waterfalls

epigraph.quote: In leveraged ETFs, liquidity is manufactured on the primary market and leased on the secondary market.
epigraph.author: ETF Capital Markets Handbook

web_blocks.html: KORU's distribution model and supply chain operate through the two-tier ETF ecosystem [1][2]. It requires no physical warehouses or enterprise sales forces [1]. On the primary market, Authorized Participants (APs) create and redeem Creation Units of 50,000 shares directly with the Trust [1][12]. In 1H FY2026 (ended April 30, 2026), APs purchased $1,139.84 million in shares and redeemed $688.89 million, generating $118.91 million in non-taxable in-kind redemption gains [8]. Those primary-market flows then reversed violently between May and July 2026 [9]. Form NPORT-P records $974.76 million in monthly redemptions in Month 1 followed by $798.40 million in share sales in Month 3 [9]. On NYSE Arca, secondary trading averaged 33.52 million shares daily across $747.35 million in November 2026 AUM [6].

KORU's upstream supply chain relies on the over-the-counter total return swap market [1]. With physical EWY holdings representing 51.3% of net assets on April 30, 2026 (57.5% on July 31), KORU sources ~230%–249% synthetic leverage from prime brokers [8][9]. By July 31, 2026, Rafferty expanded its dealer panel from four banks to seven: Bank of America, Citibank, Barclays, J.P. Morgan, BNP Paribas, UBS, and Nomura [8][9]. This broader dealer roster prevented capacity bottlenecks when AUM surged past $1.55 billion [8]. However, dealer capacity came at higher cost: April 2026 spreads widened to SOFR + 70 to 170 basis points, led by Citibank at SOFR + 1.70% and BNP Paribas at SOFR + 0.95% [8].

web_blocks.title: The Hidden Unit Cost: Prospectus AFFE vs. Audited Total Expense Ratio
paragraphs: Investors often underestimate KORU's fee drag by reviewing only Rafferty's 0.95% Operating Expense Limitation Agreement [2]. In practice, KORU bears three distinct layers of explicit cost [1][2]. First, capped fund operating expenses equal 0.95% [1][2]. This figure includes a 0.75% advisory fee, a 0.05% management service fee, and fund administration [1]. Second, Acquired Fund Fees and Expenses (AFFE) from holding EWY raise the prospectus net expense ratio to 1.32% [2][6]. Third, audited broker interest expense pushed KORU's FY2025 total net expense ratio to 1.68% of average net assets [1]. On top of these explicit costs, OTC swap contracts embed an implicit spread of SOFR plus 60 to 85 basis points [1].

web_blocks.html: From a sponsor perspective, KORU provides a high-margin, scalable fee business for Rafferty Asset Management [1]. Under Note 6 of Form N-CSR, the advisory fee is 0.75% of average daily net assets up to $1.5 billion [1]. It steps down to 0.70% between $1.5B and $2.0B, and 0.55% above $3.0B [1]. The fund also pays a 0.05% management services fee [1]. When net assets hovered near ~$20M–$26M in FY2022–FY2023, fixed costs exceeded the 0.95% expense cap and required adviser reimbursements [1]. As net assets expanded to $240.60M in FY2025 and peaked at $1,551.59M in April 2026 before moderating to $747.35M in November 2026, fixed costs shrank sharply [1][6][8]. In 1H FY2026 alone, Rafferty collected $2.40 million in net advisory fees and recouped $20,831 of prior waivers [8].

Daily rebalancing creates an invisible transaction-friction and roll-cost layer for fund holders [2][5]. Whenever KORU gains 6% during a strong Seoul trading session, its leverage ratio drops below 300% [2][5]. Portfolio managers must buy additional EWY swap notional into the 4:00 PM ET close to restore 3x exposure [1][2]. Conversely, when KORU drops 6%, managers must sell swap notional into market weakness [2][5]. Prime brokers absorb most routine execution within agreed SOFR plus 70 to 170 basis point spreads [8]. However, extreme single-day index moves force dealers to widen hedging spreads [1][5]. This dynamic subtly compounds the total cost of holding KORU through volatile macro environments [1][5].

web_blocks.title: 1H FY2026 Unit Economics Compression & 264% Turnover Friction
paragraphs: Audited FY2025 NII margin of 52.6% ($2.00M NII on $3.81M income) weakened materially in 1H FY2026 [1][8]. For the six months ended April 30, 2026, KORU earned $7.73 million in investment income ($2.10M EWY dividends plus $5.63M collateral interest) [8].

Net expenses climbed to $5.04 million—driven by $2.17 million in broker interest expense and $2.40 million in advisory fees—leaving $2.69 million in NII, or a 34.8% NII margin [8]. Simultaneously, physical-sleeve portfolio turnover jumped from 81% in FY2025 to 264% in just six months [8].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand how KORU actually works as a business—both for the sponsor that runs it and for the trader who rents it—you have to look at two different sets of unit economics side by side. On one side is Rafferty Asset Management, which collects a clean, asset-based toll. On the other side is the fund itself, which has to pay Wall Street swap dealers for leverage while earning yield on its cash collateral.

Start with the distribution and supply chain. KORU does not have a salesforce knocking on doors in Seoul or New York. Its primary-market distribution runs through Authorized Participants—institutional market makers who create and redeem large blocks of KORU shares whenever secondary-market demand on NYSE Arca pushes the trading price away from intraday net asset value. In FY2025, those in-kind redemptions generated $17.81 million in realized gains inside the fund, a structural tax shield that kept KORU from having to pass big capital-gains distributions to shareholders on its physical EWY sleeve. Meanwhile, secondary-market liquidity has become formidable: on an asset base that peaked at $1.55 billion in April 2026 and stood at $747.35 million in November 2026, KORU trades an average of 33.52 million shares a day.

Now follow the cash waterfall inside the fund itself using the audited FY2025 Statement of Operations. In fiscal year 2025, KORU collected $3.81 million in cash investment income—$1.59 million from EWY dividends and $2.22 million from Treasury and government money market interest. Against that $3.81 million, the fund paid $0.78 million in direct broker interest expense (roughly 20.5% of investment income), $0.81 million in investment advisory fees to Rafferty at the 0.75% statutory rate, and $0.22 million in net licensing, management service, and administrative costs. That left $2.00 million—or $52.60 out of every $100 of cash income—as net investment income.

That positive $2.00 million net investment income number might fool a casual reader into thinking KORU pays for itself. It does not, for two reasons you must keep front and center. First, as short-term U.S. interest rates fluctuate, the 4% money market yield that subsidized FY2025 expenses can shrink—look back to FY2021, when near-zero T-bill yields left KORU with negative net investment income of -$2.70 per share. Second, the explicit 1.68% audited net expense ratio (or 1.32% prospectus ratio including Acquired Fund Fees and Expenses from EWY) does not capture the implicit financing spread baked into the daily swap resets—SOFR plus 70 to 170 basis points across seven Wall Street dealers by July 2026—nor does it capture the quadratic volatility drag of daily rebalancing.

Think as well about the operational leverage on the other side of the table—for Rafferty Asset Management. When KORU's net assets languished at $20.09 million in FY2022 and $26.05 million in FY2023, fixed annual overhead like exchange listing fees ($10,087 in FY2025), MSCI licensing fees ($72,621), and audit fees ate into the 0.95% expense cap, forcing Rafferty to reimburse the fund. By FY2025, with net assets at $240.60 million, those same fixed costs became a rounding error—and in the six months ended April 2026 alone, as net assets reached $1.55 billion, Rafferty collected $2.40 million in advisory fees plus $155,120 in management service fees.

Finally, remember what happens at 3:55 PM Eastern Time every single day. Because KORU must reset to exactly 300% exposure, every up-day forces the fund to buy more swap notional into the close, and every down-day forces it to sell swap notional into the close. That daily 'buy high, sell low' mechanical flow is the hidden supply-chain friction of all leveraged ETFs: it guarantees 3x exposure for tomorrow morning's open, but it turns every choppy week into a slow leak of capital.

The April 30, 2026 semi-annual report proves that KORU's FY2025 cash-income cushion was unusually fragile. In the first half of FY2026, total investment income jumped to $7.73 million, yet broker interest expense surged to $2.17 million and advisory fees hit $2.40 million. Total net expenses of $5.04 million ate up 65.2% of investment income, compressing KORU's net investment income margin from 52.6% in FY2025 down to 34.8%. With money market funds yielding 3.52%–3.55% against a 3.91% SOFR benchmark plus 70 to 170 basis points in swap spreads, the cash sleeve no longer fully subsidizes leverage costs.

Even more striking is the creation-redemption churn disclosed in 2026 filings. Because APs surged $1.14 billion into KORU while redeeming $688.89 million in the six months through April—and then pulled $974.76 million in May before adding $798.40 million in July—KORU's physical portfolio turnover exploded from 81% in FY2025 to 264% in just six months. Every wave of forced physical EWY creation and redemption adds bid-ask friction and tracking slippage on top of daily derivative resets.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The unit economics of KORU reveal a classic asymmetry between sponsor and holder. For Rafferty Asset Management, scaling KORU from $20 million in FY2022 to $240.6 million in FY2025 and nearly $1 billion in 2026 turns an 80-basis-point fee stream into a high-margin annuity. For the fund holder, every 1% of explicit fee plus swap spread is compounded against daily path variance—meaning the true cost of ownership is low over a three-day swing and punishing over a choppy three-year hold.

section_takeaway: In 1H FY2026, higher broker interest ($2.17M) and wider swap spreads (SOFR+70–170 bps) compressed KORU's NII margin from 52.6% to 34.8%, while flow whip-saws drove 6-month portfolio turnover to 264% [8][9].
